newsitem.title: GERMANY: Zaire force contributors to meet in Germany.
newsitem.headline: Zaire force contributors to meet in Germany.

text.p: Countries planning to send troops to Zaire will meet in Germany on Wednesday to review the force's size and mandate now that Rwandan refugees are going home, the U.S. military said on Sunday.

"A group of military planners led by the Canadians will meet in Stuttgart at the joint task force facility," U.S. Navy Captain Tim Taylor, director of public affairs for the U.S. European command based in Stuttgart, told Reuters.
Taylor said an advance team of Canadian officials had arrived in Stuttgart to plan the meeting.

"We are providing the facility for this meeting but the Canadians are leading the multinational planning effort," said Taylor, spokesman for the U.S. military headquarters that controls U.S. forces in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

About 1,000 U.S. ground troops -- including some 600 paratroopers from Italy -- were due to be sent to Zaire to help around 1.5 million refugees, mainly ethnic Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
But the mass migration of Hutu refugees back to Rwanda in the last couple of days has lessened and perhaps ended the need for a costly multinational force.
By the time the first foreign troops may be ready to deploy next week, more than half the 1.1 million Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire are likely to have returned home voluntarily.

U.S. troops were expected to provide security at the Goma airport in Zaire and along a three-mile (five km) corridor from the airport into the Rwandan city of Kigali, and also provide support to humanitarian rescue efforts, the officials said.
The U.N. special envoy on the Zaire crisis, Raymond Chretien, argued on Sunday that a military force was still needed in the region.

But South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki told a news conference at the World Food Summit in Rome that his country agreed with other African states that the terms of the multi-national mission needed to be changed.
His comments also reflected dissatisfaction among Africans with the way the U.N.-sponsored force had been organised and came amid other indications that the operation might be rethought.
Mbeki said the Canadian-led force should "be decided by the nature of the problem", adding: "We do not need the sort of numbers that have been spoken of in the past."
Leaders of some countries from Africa's Great Lake region met at the Rome summit on Saturday.

"One of the decisions that they took, with which we agree, was that in the light of the movement of refugees into Rwanda it will be necessary to review the mandate of that multinational force," Mbeki said.

"We will then, of course, take advantage of that (Stuttgart meeting)...to have some assessment of how many refugees remain in Zaire and then what kind of response is required to deal with whoever might be remaining," he said.
"But I think one of the urgent questions that remains is that you've got these refugees who might have shifted location and are now in Rwanda and who still need to be fed and clothed," Mbeki said.
Rwandan Prime Minister Pierre Celestine Rwigema told the summit on Saturday that the force should be scrapped, and its budget spent instead on re-settling the refugees in his country.
Burundi's Prime Minister Pascale Firmin Ndimira said the force was needed but suggested it be more actively involved in bringing the refugees home and not simply help with aid.
Kenya and other African countries have complained that they were not consulted properly before the U.N. Security Council approved the force last week.
